subject: Biotechnology
title: Carbon Capture by Microbes
description: A 60-second lesson on Carbon Capture by Microbes.

hook.text: What if factories emitted food instead of pollution? Engineered microbes can convert CO2 into useful chemicals.

buildup.text: LanzaTech uses Clostridium bacteria to ferment industrial CO2 and CO emissions into ethanol — waste gas becomes fuel.

discovery.text: Autotrophic bacteria fix CO2 using hydrogen — producing proteins, plastics, and fuels from thin air and renewable energy.

twist.text: Scaling gas fermentation is tricky — gas-liquid mass transfer limits how fast microbes can consume CO2 in large reactors.

climax.text: Solarfoods' Solein grows protein from CO2, water, and electricity — food from air, approved for sale in Singapore.

punchline.text: Feed microbes CO2, harvest value — biology turns emissions into products.

quiz.question: How does LanzaTech's process convert industrial emissions into fuel?
options: It burns emissions at high temperatures to produce synthetic gasoline
Clostridium bacteria ferment CO and CO2 from industrial waste gas into ethanol
It uses chemical catalysts to split CO2 into carbon and oxygen

details.summary: Certain microorganisms naturally capture and convert CO2 into useful products through photosynthesis or chemosynthesis. Engineered microbes can be optimized to sequester carbon while producing biofuels, bioplastics, or industrial chemicals from captured greenhouse gas.
details.whyItMatters: Microbial carbon capture could turn industrial CO2 emissions from a waste problem into a feedstock for valuable products. It offers a biological complement to mechanical carbon capture with potentially lower energy costs.
takeaways: Photosynthetic microalgae naturally convert CO2 into biomass and oils
Engineered bacteria can fix carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals
Microbial capture can be paired with industrial exhaust as a CO2 source

faq.question: How efficient are microbes at capturing carbon dioxide?
faq.answer: Microalgae fix CO2 roughly 10 times faster than terrestrial plants per unit area. Engineered autotrophic bacteria can be even faster. However, harvesting biomass and converting it to stable products requires energy that partially offsets the carbon benefit.

faq.question: Can microbial carbon capture work at industrial scale?
faq.answer: Pilot plants pairing algae cultivation with power plant exhaust show promise. Challenges include managing large volumes of water, preventing contamination, and ensuring net-negative carbon when full lifecycle emissions are counted.
